title: BlackRock Says India Has Been 'Over-Punished.' Record Outflows May Have Run Their Course.
excerpt: The world's largest asset manager sees India as a top emerging-market conviction — even after $30 billion in foreign money fled and market cap fell behind Taiwan and South Korea
body:
The world's largest asset manager has a message for investors who have been fleeing India: you have gone too far.

BlackRock, which manages more than $14 trillion in assets globally, said this week that India's equity market has been "over-punished" for lacking a direct AI play and for the oil price risks brought on by the Iran war. The firm called India one of its highest-conviction, medium- to long-term emerging market trades.

The endorsement arrives at a painful moment. India's market capitalisation has slipped below both Taiwan and South Korea this year as global investors chased semiconductor and chipmaker stocks — the hardware backbone of the AI boom. The Nifty 50 and Sensex have dropped 11 per cent and 13 per cent respectively in 2026. Foreign investors have pulled out a record $30 billion from Indian equities, putting the country on course to far surpass last year's record $18.9 billion divestment.

## From Darling to Seventh Place

India's share in the MSCI Global Standard index has shrunk to 12.3 per cent from a peak of 21 per cent in September 2024. Without the equivalent of a TSMC or an SK Hynix, the conventional wisdom says, capital will not come back anytime soon.

"The rotation has gone too far," said Natasha Sarkaria, BlackRock's EMEA investment strategy lead of wealth. "It doesn't mean there are no derivative AI stories in India."

Lighthouse Canton, a global wealth and asset management firm with more than $5 billion under management, echoed the argument. Abhay Laijawala, the firm's India chief investment officer, called India's absence from the AI hardware trade an "advantage of absence."

"We have plenty of picks and shovels," he told Reuters, pointing to India's deep listed universe in power generation, data centres, electrical equipment, cooling systems, engineering, and capital goods — the physical infrastructure that underpins every AI deployment.

## The Case for Patience

BlackRock's conviction rests on fundamentals that the selloff has obscured. India's economy grew a stronger-than-expected 7.8 per cent in the March quarter. The firm sees low double-digit earnings growth for the MSCI India index this year. It remains positive on financials, industrials, materials, utilities, and consumer discretionary stocks.

"As long as India's GDP grows between 6 and 7 per cent, that's a nice sweet spot for the economy to keep growing, keep expanding," Sarkaria said.

The Reserve Bank of India has helped the case. This month it eased overseas borrowing rules for lenders, sending bank stocks surging. Kotak Mahindra Bank, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank all gained between 3 and 7 per cent in the week ending Friday. The Nifty snapped a two-week losing streak.

## What It Means for NRI Investors

For the millions of NRIs with portfolios weighted towards India — through direct equity holdings, mutual funds, or NRE fixed deposits — BlackRock's position offers a counterpoint to months of grim headlines. The firm is not calling an all-clear. It acknowledges that higher oil prices, a weaker rupee, and rising input costs will pressure corporate profitability over the next two quarters.

But the thesis is that India's structural story — demographics, infrastructure spending, financial deepening, and now indirect AI-linked opportunities — remains intact beneath the short-term pain. Friday's market rally, the best session in two months on hopes of a US-Iran peace deal, offered a glimpse of what a macro improvement could do.

South Korea and Taiwan have both logged foreign outflows in June, suggesting some investors have begun trimming crowded AI positions. If that rotation accelerates, the money has to go somewhere. BlackRock is betting a meaningful share of it comes back to India.

Sources: Reuters, BlackRock, Lighthouse Canton, LiveMint
